blocks.text: Organisms require nutrition for their survival and maintenance. A nutrient is a substance that provides the body with the essential ingredients required for metabolism. Specific nutrients such as carbohydrates, lipids and proteins serve as sources of energy; others, including water, electrolytes, minerals and vitamins, are necessary for the metabolic process. Nutrition refers to the collective processes involved in the intake and use of nutrients for growth, repair and the maintenance of activities in an organism.

All autotrophic organisms need carbon dioxide and water, which supply carbon, oxygen and hydrogen, the predominant elements required for making organic molecules. Plants get many other nutrients from the environment, and these fall into two groups. Macronutrients are needed in relatively larger amounts: there are nine, namely carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium and sulphur. Micronutrients are needed in very small amounts: there are seven, namely iron, manganese, zinc, molybdenum, copper, chlorine and boron.

blocks.title: Fertilisers
blocks.text: Fertilisers are added to the soil to provide macronutrients and micronutrients to crops.

blocks.title: Manganese and stress
blocks.text: Manganese is important for the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), which help to mitigate oxidative stress in plants under adverse environmental conditions.

Some plants supplement their food with organic molecules in addition to inorganic nutrients, acquired by capturing and breaking down insects and tiny animals. All insectivorous plants are true autotrophs, but their development accelerates when they capture prey; the nitrogenous compounds of the animal body are evidently of benefit. The captured insects are broken down by enzymes released by the leaves. The pitcher plant, Venus fly trap and sundew are well-known insectivorous plants.

items: Pitcher plant: the leaves are modified into a sac or pitcher partly filled with water. The terminal part of the leaf forms a hood that partly covers the opening, and numerous stiff hairs prevent little insects from crawling out once they have fallen in.

blocks.alt: A leaf blade whose tip continues as a curling tendril into a green pitcher. The pitcher has a red rim and a lid-like Hood above its mouth; stiff hairs on its inner wall point downward; its lower part is filled with water in which two insects are trapped. Labels: Hood, Pitcher, Stiff hairs, Water, Trapped insect, Leaf.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.1: Pitcher plant, insects are entrapped within the leaf (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.1).

items: Venus fly trap: the trap is two lobes hinged at the end of each leaf. The inner surfaces carry trichomes, hair-like projections that trigger the lobes to close rapidly on contact with prey. Fine bristles along the hinged traps interlock on closure so the prey cannot escape; it is digested by enzymes secreted from glands on the leaf surface and the products are absorbed.

blocks.alt: Left: an open trap at the end of a winged leaf stalk, two red lobes joined at a midrib hinge, with stiff bristles along the edges and a few yellow trichomes on the inner surface. Right: a closed trap with the bristles interlocked and an insect caught inside. Labels: Bristles, Trichomes, Lobe, Hinge, Leaf stalk, Trapped prey, Closed trap.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.2: Venus-fly trap, prey is trapped between the lobes of a leaf (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.2).

items: Sundew: catches prey with shiny drops of dew, from which its name comes. The leaves are covered with tiny tentacle-like hairs, each with a gland and a single drop of dew at the tip. Insects attracted by the plant's odour are trapped by the tentacles, digested by enzymes, and the products absorbed.

blocks.alt: A round green leaf on a stalk, ringed by many red tentacle-like hairs, each tipped with a shining dew drop; shorter glandular hairs cover the leaf. On the right the tentacles bend over an insect stuck to them. Labels: Dew drop, Tentacles, Leaf, Trapped insect.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.3: Sundew, insects are entangled by the tentacles (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.3).
